recipe_title: Southwestern Chicken and Black Bean Mason Jar Salad

details.title_candidate: Southwestern Chicken and Black Bean Mason Jar Salad

warnings: Stage 4 coverage: 'extra-virgin olive oil': [748608] Oil, olive, extra virgin has no USDA value for fiber_g, protein_g (which would be summed as zero) — switched to [171413] Oil, olive, salad or cooking.

[thirty_minute_practicality] The recipe relies on 'cooked and cooled' quinoa. Cooking and cooling raw quinoa from scratch takes longer than 30 minutes. To honestly meet the book's 30-minute cold-start promise, update the ingredient text to say 'leftover or store-bought pre-cooked pouch quinoa'. It would also be helpful to specify 'cooked chicken breast (such as rotisserie)'.

details.summary: An excellent, highly practical mason jar salad that perfectly hits the nutritional targets and culinary goals of the book. Just explicitly note the use of leftover or pre-cooked pouch quinoa in the ingredients list to maintain total transparency regarding the 30-minute time promise.

dimensions.feedback: Classic Southwestern flavor profile with a bright lime and cumin vinaigrette. The flavors are well-balanced, punchy, and make perfect culinary sense together.
Every listed ingredient is accurately accounted for in the step-by-step assembly instructions.
The assembly instructions are clear and properly explain the layered mason jar technique to ensure the delicate greens remain crisp.
Perfectly aligned with Southwestern cuisine, utilizing black beans, corn, cumin, fresh cilantro, and lime.
The mason jar assembly method is ideal for a prep-ahead lunch salad, brilliantly keeping the wet dressing and heavy ingredients at the bottom away from the lettuce.
The nutrition values align perfectly with the given ingredients and quantities. The high protein and quality carbohydrate counts compute properly.
The title and intro accurately and attractively describe the dish without resorting to any banned health claims, 'detox', or gimmicky language.
A highly appealing, colorful, and genuinely practical weekday lunch that readers will look forward to eating.

An excellent example of eating for both conditions: lean protein, exceptional fiber from legumes and vegetables, and a vibrant dressing built on heart-healthy extra-virgin olive oil rather than saturated fats.

Zero added sugar, with a robust, high-quality carbohydrate component (34.6 g) coming entirely from whole foods (beans, corn, quinoa, tomatoes). It lands squarely in the middle of the chapter's target window.
Hits every single target for a 'light main' salad. Protein (35.1 g), fiber (9.1 g), and carbs (34.6 g) are perfectly dialed in, and the vinaigrette is made from scratch as required.

The recipe relies on 'cooked and cooled' quinoa. Cooking and cooling raw quinoa from scratch takes longer than 30 minutes. To honestly meet the book's 30-minute cold-start promise, update the ingredient text to say 'leftover or store-bought pre-cooked pouch quinoa'. It would also be helpful to specify 'cooked chicken breast (such as rotisserie)'.
